issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, these two items directly contradict each other: being able to talk about the trauma very easily is inconsistent with losing the thread and being unable to finish when trying to explain it. Partial clarity could coexist with fragmented recall, but not with both easy verbal access and marked inability to narrate the event.

vignette: Caleb's experience began in a remote canyon during a solo topographical survey when men in dark vehicles ambushed him, bound him, and held him in a windowless room for days. The captors controlled every variable: they decided when food arrived, when doors unlatched, and deliberately stretched pauses to keep him off balance. They applied calculated physical pressure to his limbs and ribs, leaving him with lasting stiffness and a constant awareness of his own fragility. He could not call for help, and his pleas were met with silence or threats that reinforced his powerlessness. When he returned to his patrol routes, the changes arrived quickly and without warning. His chest would tighten, his breath would shallow, and his muscles would coil before his mind had even registered a threat. In the ranger station, a delayed radio check or a maintenance vehicle taking longer than usual to clear the access road made his shoulders hike up and his pulse hammer against his ribs. An extended wait, whether for a supply drop or a colleague's reply, felt like a countdown to another kind of confinement. His hands would drift to the station doors and windows, turning the deadbolts and latches until the clicks felt final, then turning them again. He had come to believe that his body had been permanently damaged by what happened, that the lingering aches and sudden tremors were proof his frame was fundamentally compromised. This conviction sat alongside a quiet certainty that he could not rely on other people to keep him safe. He stopped asking for rides to distant trailheads, stopped leaving his house key with his supervisor, and withdrew from casual contact, convinced that dependence was a structural flaw in his approach to survival. His erratic sleep, his startle responses, his sudden flatness in conversation-all of it read to him as evidence that his mind was fraying, that he was going crazy. He was certain that if he lost control even once more, he would not recover. The memories themselves refused to settle into a coherent sequence. Some hours remained razor-sharp-the groan of a specific hinge, the smell of damp concrete, the weight of restraints against his forearms-while entire stretches dissolved into white noise. When supervisors or family asked him to describe what had happened, he would start speaking, only to lose the thread, his mouth going dry as the story fractured into fragments he could not piece together. He found himself unable to put the frightening event into words at all. Alongside these gaps, Caleb started scripting his days. Before stepping onto the radio, before answering a hiker's question at the trailhead, he ran through possible exchanges in his head, rehearsing exact phrasing to keep interactions safe and contained. The emotional dam followed as a separate measure; when feelings threatened to breach the surface, he forced himself blank, watching the world through a pane of glass. The patrol truck became a site of acute tension. Sitting behind the wheel or in the passenger seat made his breath catch, his hands gripping the door frame as if bracing for another kind of captivity. He began taking longer foot routes, refusing rides to remote survey sites, and eventually started requesting administrative duty. The work required more hours, the trail logs grew incomplete, and his supervisor's calls went unanswered. What frightened him most was the slow erosion of his own competence, the way a single missed shift spiraled into a handoff of his radio that felt like surrender. He sat on the intake bench, palms sweating, wondering if the evaluation itself would be another test of his endurance. He hoped for a way to stop the constant rehearsal, to trust that a locked door was just a door, to find a version of himself that didn't require numbness to survive the day. Most of all, he feared another collapse, another loss of control, and quietly wished for a path that didn't demand he choose between his safety and his own mind.
